pr_body:
Addresses several problems with accepting incoming connections:
- pending connections now don't get queued until the handshake is finished (whether successfully or not)
  - `ListenBacklog` limit is enforced manually via `_pendingConnectionsCapacity`
  - in case of listener disposal, the active handshakes get stopped via `_disposeCts`
  - `PendingConnection` class is now irrelevant thus removed, `_acceptQueue` either contains `QuicConnection` or an `Exception`
- unexpected exception from handshake timeout is now wrapped in `QuicException`
  - this is straightforward solution without any regards to planned exception revisions where we should revisit this particular change (#82262)

Fixes #77310
Fixes #80172
Contributes to #78096

issue_context.title: Possible QuicConnection leak
issue_context.body:
This method is called during the disposal of the listener.

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/88f75a83803a3b7fe59bcdb3eb748eefa4d35ddb/src/libraries/System.Net.Quic/src/System/Net/Quic/QuicListener.PendingConnection.cs#L99

If the _finishHandshakeTask task has already been completed successfully the QuicConnection held by this task is never disposed of, and this is the only reference left to it.

Triage: looks like a legitimate bug, we should confirm this and fix it. It should be fairly simple fix.

There seems to be a similar issue any time `PendingConnection.FinishHandshakeAsync` gets canceled. While not ideal, hopefully the `MsQuicContextSafeHandle` at least cleans things up in either case, right?
Yep and yep, problem is the same with cancellation, and `MsQuicContextSafeHandle` cleans up eventually, after GC collects the main object.

review_comments: log? May be handy for debug. and may be worth of counter.

Good point. For counters, we should probably do overall walk through S.N.Quic and design and expose more of them.

BTW, this, at least, gets propagated to the client, so it won't get silently swallowed.
we may check that `clientConnection2` can still be accepted. e.g. failure of `clientConnection3` does not impact `clientConnection3`.

Do we really want to do it? For TCP the accept does not return any failed connections. While this may be handy for debugging, I'm worried about DoS when somebody can flood init attempt and we would go to throwing/catching game making it way more expensive IMHO. I would suggest log and silent discard ASAP.

cc: @JamesNK @Tratcher for any more thoughts.

Kestrel stops listening to `QuicListener.AcceptConnectionAsync` if the methods throws:
1. `QuickException` with `QuicError.OperationAborted`
2. `ObjectDisposedException`
3. `OperationCanceledException` triggered by canceling the passed-in token.

Anything else is logged, and Kestrel calls accept again.

This has been discussed and changed and is nothing new in this PR, see https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/72160#issuecomment-1184127586, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/72161#issuecomment-1184138201 and the PR https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72390. Silently discarding errors was causing troubles diagnosing some problems.

TCP may not give you failed accept attempts, but errors from establishing SSL on top of that would get propagated, wouldn't they? And this is more like that IMHO. Note that this exception get here only intentionally from `StartConnectionHandshake` and these are the cases:
- options validation failed, i.e. user provided wrong options on the callback, including errors from preparing `MsQuicConfiguration`, this is a way to let them know
- TLS handshake failed for any reason, i.e. an error coming from MsQuic
- handshake timeout expired (10 seconds), i.e our own imposed as MsQuic would never kill that connection in this state: https://github.com/microsoft/msquic/discussions/2705

On top of that, we are actively refusing any connection attempts over `ListenBacklog` count, without even starting the handshake. Which is something we didn't do in 6.0 where we discarded that connection only after we fully established it. 

We can fine tune the cases when we propagate the errors, but I wouldn't discard them all, that's something that's been intentionally fixed.

I'm not convinced about the arguments, but I can live with the outcome. We should also update https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.quic.quiclistener.acceptconnectionasync?view=net-7.0 and perhaps be specific what exceptions `AcceptConnectionAsync` can throw. 

For background, AAD has benchmark to measure how expensive it is to handle failed connections/requests. And I think the DoS scenarios are real e.g. cost of error handling. But it can perhaps still be small comparing to cost of the crypto.
any reason why don't leave it as Bounded channel?
We impose the limits in a different fashion via `_pendingConnectionsCapacity` so no need to keep it bounded. And unbounded is more performant as it doesn't need to check the limits.

I was mostly wondering if we could still relay on the channel counting instead of introducing new mechanisms. Bit it seems like you count immediately after the even and we also account the failures.
I think that is fine, we should be clear about it in https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.quic.quiclisteneroptions.listenbacklog?view=net-7.0#system-net-quic-quiclisteneroptions-listenbacklog as it differs from TCP e.g. may surprise callers.
